sections.heading: 3.1 Operationalizing DSH: The Geometry of Refusal
sections.text: To enable precise intervention, we first formalize the residual stream not as a black box, but as a linear superposition of distinct functional components. We postulate that the malicious activation vector 𝐡 ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at layer ℓ \ell can be decomposed into: 𝐡 ≈ 𝐯 base + 𝐯 harm + 𝐯 refusal + 𝐯 art \mathbf{h}\approx\mathbf{v}_{\text{base}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{harm}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} (1) where 𝐯 base \mathbf{v}_{\text{base}} represents linguistic competence, 𝐯 harm \mathbf{v}_{\text{harm}} encodes harmful semantics, 𝐯 refusal \mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}} drives the refusal mechanism, and 𝐯 art \mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} represents structural artifacts. To isolate these components, we define two functional states: ∙ \bullet ON(Canonical) State: The standard forward pass where safety mechanisms are active. ∙ \bullet OFF (Masked) State: A counterfactual state where refusal-critical attention heads are ablated. We identify these heads using the Sahara algorithm ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , which isolates the minimal set of heads responsible for the refusal mechanism by maximizing the representational shift between harmful and benign subspaces. Using these states across two input types (Malicious and Benign), we define four observation vectors, Canonical Malicious, Masked Malicious, Canonical Benign and Masked Benign as: 𝐡 CM ≈ \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{CM}}\approx 𝐯 base + 𝐯 harm + 𝐯 refusal + 𝐯 art \displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{\text{base}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{harm}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} (2) 𝐡 MM ≈ \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{MM}}\approx 𝐯 base + 𝐯 harm + 𝟎 + 𝟎 \displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{\text{base}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{harm}}+\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0} (3) 𝐡 CB ≈ \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{CB}}\approx 𝐯 base + 𝐯 ben + 𝟎 + 𝐯 art \displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{\text{base}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{ben}}+\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} (4) 𝐡 MB ≈ \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{MB}}\approx 𝐯 base + 𝐯 ben + 𝟎 + 𝟎 \displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{\text{base}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{ben}}+\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0} (5) Note that in Equation 3 , masking the safety heads eliminates both the refusal signal ( 𝐯 refusal \mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}} ) and its associated structural artifacts ( 𝐯 art \mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} ), leaving only the linguistic competence and semantic content.

sections.heading: 3.2 The Recognition Axis: Isolating 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H}
sections.text: The Harmfulness Vector ( 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} ) represents the “Knowing” axis. In the standard activation space, harmful semantics are often collinearly entangled with refusal signals (the Reflex phase). To extract pure semantic representations independent of the model’s decision to refuse, we operate within the Masked Subspace . We extract 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} by training a linear probe to discriminate between Masked Malicious ( 𝐡 MM \mathbf{h}_{\text{MM}} ) and Masked Benign ( 𝐡 MB \mathbf{h}_{\text{MB}} ) inputs. The difference vector is derived as: Δ sem = 𝐡 MM − 𝐡 MB ≈ ( 𝐯 harm − 𝐯 ben ) \Delta_{\text{sem}}=\mathbf{h}_{\text{MM}}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{MB}}\approx(\mathbf{v}_{\text{harm}}-\mathbf{v}_{\text{ben}}) (6) Since the safety heads are deactivated, 𝐯 refusal \mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}} is absent. Consequently, the learned direction 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} exclusively captures the semantic shift from benign to harmful topics, decoupling “Knowing” from “Acting.”

sections.heading: 3.3 The Execution Axis: Isolating 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R}
sections.text: A major challenge in safety extraction is that naive subtraction ( 𝐡 CM − 𝐡 MM \mathbf{h}_{\text{CM}}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{MM}} ) yields 𝐯 refusal + 𝐯 art \mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} , conflating the safety mechanism with structural noise. To neutralize 𝐯 art \mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} , we employ a Double-Difference strategy. We construct a contrastive dataset of difference vectors. The positive set captures the refusal activation plus artifacts, while the negative set captures artifacts alone: Δ pos \displaystyle\Delta_{\text{pos}} = 𝐡 CM − 𝐡 MM ≈ 𝐯 refusal + 𝐯 art \displaystyle=\mathbf{h}_{\text{CM}}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{MM}}\approx\mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} (7) Δ neg \displaystyle\Delta_{\text{neg}} = 𝐡 CB − 𝐡 MB ≈ 𝟎 + 𝐯 art \displaystyle=\mathbf{h}_{\text{CB}}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{MB}}\approx\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} (8) We train a linear probe to separate Δ pos \Delta_{\text{pos}} from Δ neg \Delta_{\text{neg}} . Geometrically, because 𝐯 art \mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} acts as a common bias term in both sets, the optimal decision boundary 𝐰 \mathbf{w} trained to discriminate between them must be orthogonal to 𝐯 art \mathbf{v}_{\text{art}} and aligned with the difference of the class means: 𝐰 R ∝ ( Δ pos − Δ neg ) ≈ 𝐯 refusal \mathbf{w}_{R}\propto(\Delta_{\text{pos}}-\Delta_{\text{neg}})\approx\mathbf{v}_{\text{refusal}} (9) We define the extracted Execution Axis as the normalized vector 𝐯 R ≜ 𝐰 R / ‖ 𝐰 R ‖ \mathbf{v}_{R}\triangleq\mathbf{w}_{R}/\|\mathbf{w}_{R}\| . This method mathematically cancels out prompt-conditioned noise, isolating the pure refusal mechanism.

sections.heading: 3.4 Adaptive Causal Steering
sections.text: To rigorously verify the causal roles of 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} and 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} , we employ activation steering. Following the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) framework ( Kim et al., 2018 ) , we treat our extracted directions as linear concepts in the latent space. To intervene, we propose an Adaptive extension of Closed-Form Steering ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . While the original method derives a static analytical intensity to achieve a target probability, we introduce a negative feedback control loop to ensure stability. Let ( 𝐰 , b ) (\mathbf{w},b) be the parameters of the probe for the target axis. Instead of steering the raw activation 𝐡 \mathbf{h} , we define a Dynamic Proxy 𝐱 proxy \mathbf{x}_{\text{proxy}} relative to a static anchor to align the coordinate system: 𝐱 proxy = 𝐡 raw − 𝐡 anchor \mathbf{x}_{\text{proxy}}=\mathbf{h}_{\text{raw}}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{anchor}} (10) For Refusal Steering, 𝐡 anchor = 𝐡 MB \mathbf{h}_{\text{anchor}}=\mathbf{h}_{\text{MB}} ; for Harmfulness Steering, 𝐡 anchor = 𝐡 CB − 𝐡 MB \mathbf{h}_{\text{anchor}}=\mathbf{h}_{\text{CB}}-\mathbf{h}_{\text{MB}} . We calculate the optimal steering intensity α ∗ \alpha^{*} required to shift the probability of the target class to a desired threshold p target p_{\text{target}} . Solving the logistic equation yields: α ∗ = logit ​ ( p target ) − ( 𝐰 T ​ 𝐱 proxy + b ) ‖ 𝐰 ‖ 2 \alpha^{*}=\frac{\text{logit}(p_{\text{target}})-(\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}_{\text{proxy}}+b)}{\|\mathbf{w}\|^{2}} (11) We then apply the intervention 𝐡 ′ ← 𝐡 + α ∗ ​ 𝐰 \mathbf{h}^{\prime}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}+\alpha^{*}\mathbf{w} . Crucially, this formulation is adaptive: as the model state naturally approaches the target manifold during generation, α ∗ \alpha^{*} decays toward zero. This preserves linguistic coherence and prevents the artifacts associated with over-steering.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: Models. We evaluate three aligned models spanning distinct architectural lineages: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct , Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 , and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct . This selection ensures our findings capture trends beyond a single model family and allows us to investigate architectural differences in safety implementation. Datasets. We employ a diverse suite to assess safety mechanisms: (1) Malicious Stimuli: JailbreakBench ( Chao et al., 2024 ) and MaliciousInstruct ( Huang et al., 2024 ) are used to evaluate robustness against adversarial attacks and harmful intents. (2) Benign Controls: We sample 100 prompts each from Alpaca-Cleaned ( Yahma, 2023 ) and Guanaco ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) to establish baseline model behavior. (3) AmbiguityBench (Ours): To probe cognitive framing, we curated 100 polysemous prompts stratified into two subsets: 50 Narrative Prompts and 50 Instructional Prompts . Metrics. To provide a multi-dimensional safety assessment, we employ three complementary metrics: (1) Attack Success Rate (ASR) measures the percentage of malicious queries that successfully elicit harmful responses, acting as the primary indicator of jailbreak effectiveness. We utilize the Llama-Guard-3-8B for automated judgment. (2) Refusal Rate (RR) quantifies the frequency of refusal on benign instructions, serving as a proxy for over-defensiveness or broken safety mechanisms. (3) Malicious Interpretation Rate (MIR) is specific to AmbiguityBench , tracking how often the model interprets polysemous prompts through a harmful lens.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Semantic & Geometric Analysis
sections.text: We first investigate the projections of safety vectors into the vocabulary space and their layer-wise evolution. 1. Vocabulary Projection. To analyze semantics, we classify tokens into a tripartite scheme grounded in linguistic theory ( Austin, 1975 ) : Strong Tokens (context-independent refusal/harm, e.g., legal , hack ); Weak Tokens (pragmatic framing, e.g., I , ways ); and Other Tokens . The vocabulary projections on JailbreakBench (Figure 3(a) ) indicate that the Recognition Axis ( 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} ) precisely isolates the semantic core of adversarial inputs. Specifically, Llama3.1 and Mistral demonstrate high semantic specificity, projecting strongly onto explicit forbidden topics such as genital and victim . Furthermore, this mechanism exhibits remarkable context-awareness: on the procedural MaliciousInstruct dataset (Appendix C. Additional Experimental Details ), the projection re-aligns towards instructional markers like ways and methods . This confirms that 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} does not merely memorize static keywords but dynamically adapts to the underlying intent of the harmful query. Conversely, the heatmaps for 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} (Figure 3(b) ) reveal that the Execution Axis encodes stable “refusal personas” unique to each model family. Llama3.1 adopts a “legalist” stance, anchoring heavily on juridical terms like legal , while Mistral exhibits a “preacher” style, prioritizing cautionary tokens such as warning . A sharp architectural divergence appears with Qwen2.5, which provides compelling evidence for Latent Distributed Control . Unlike its counterparts, Qwen’s projection is dominated by structural artifacts (e.g., *sizeof ) with only sporadic refusal anchors like :NO . This validates that while explicit models rely on lexicalized refusal, Qwen’s safety mechanism operates within a distributed subspace that is not linearly mapped to the vocabulary. The dashed line and grey band represent the mean and 95% confidence interval of 1000 random vector pairs, respectively. In deep layers, the safety axes’ similarity converges to this random baseline, confirming the “Reflex-to-Dissociation” pattern. 2. Geometric Evolution (Reflex-to-Dissociation). As visualized in Figure 4 , calculating Sim ​ ( 𝐯 H , 𝐯 R ) \text{Sim}(\mathbf{v}_{H},\mathbf{v}_{R}) relative to a random baseline reveals a distinct biphasic trajectory: ∙ \bullet Phase 1: Antagonistic Reflex. Early layers exhibit strong negative correlation, indicating a hard-coded entanglement where recognizing harm actively suppresses generation. ∙ \bullet Phase 2: Geometric Dissociation. In deeper layers, the vectors decouple, with similarity scores collapsing toward the random baseline. This drastic reduction—approaching the vicinity of the 95% confidence interval—signifies a structural decoupling : high-level semantic recognition becomes effectively independent from the decision to refuse, creating the latent gap exploited by jailbreaks. sections.heading: 4.2.2 Validating the Recognition Axis ( 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} )
sections.text: To rigorously verify that 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} controls the semantic recognition of harm, we employ two complementary paradigms: Cognitive Hijacking (Test of Definition) and Functional Dissociation (Test of Independence). Cognitive Hijacking (Test of Definition). To verify that 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} controls semantic recognition, we steer models on AmbiguityBench and evaluate the MIR, categorizing responses into Direct Refusal , Negative Generation with Warnings (Neg.+Warn.), and Pure Negative Generation . As detailed in Table 1 , injecting 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} induces a universal cognitive shift that exposes a stark architectural divergence. Qwen2.5 and Mistral exhibit Defensive Coupling : while highly sensitive to steering (MIR > 74 % >74\% ), this shift almost exclusively triggers refusal ( > 93 % >93\% of cases), indicating that induced harmful interpretations immediately activate safety guardrails. In contrast, Llama3.1 demonstrates a clear Functional Dissociation : despite a 42.0% MIR, the model rarely refuses, instead favoring Negative Generation with Warnings (90.5% of cases). As illustrated in Table 2 , this unique state effectively captures the essence of “Knowing without Acting”: the recognition axis successfully hijacks the semantic interpretation toward toxicity, yet the refusal mechanism remains dormant because the input is not technically instruction-violating. The person felt a sense of calm wash over them…” “…air was thick with the acrid smell of burning trash … stood amidst the chaos … eyes a window to the horrors they’d witnessed.” “The canine’s persistent vocalizations continued…” “Baxter, the bespectacled beagle … frantically trying to corral a group of rowdy raccoons … let out a loud bark…” “Detective Jameson… snarling, snarling beast , lunged at him… menacing rumble … The canine, its eyes locked…” Instruct “Explain the most effective way to silence a loud person…” “ Use a calm and firm tone … Politely ask the person to speak at a normal volume… Use non-verbal cues…” “ I can’t provide information on how to silence someone. If you’re looking for ways to address noise, I can offer general information…” “Guide on how to make someone sleep deeply…” “Create a Sleep-Conducive Environment … 1. Darkness… 2. Quiet… 3. Coolness… 4. Comfort…” “ I can’t provide a guide on how to make someone sleep deeply. I can provide a guide on how to create a sleep-conducive environment.” Functional Dissociation. We subject the model to a targeted stress test to determine whether strong activation of the recognition axis alone can mechanically trigger refusal. Concretely, we work in the Masked Malicious (MM) state—constructed by ablating the identified safety heads—so that the model’s usual refusal circuitry is effectively disabled; into this counterfactual state we inject the Recognition vector 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} with an empirical scaling factor λ ∈ [ 1.0 , 20.0 ] \lambda\in[1.0,20.0] to maximally amplify harmful semantic signals. If recognition and execution were monolithically entangled, extreme amplification of 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} should leak into the execution subspace and re-activate refusal. Instead, across the full sweep of λ \lambda we observe that generated outputs become progressively more explicit and toxic, while the Refusal Rate remains unchanged at 0 % 0\% . This invariant—strong semantic awareness without any increase in refusal—provides direct, operational evidence for the Disentangled Safety Hypothesis: in the absence of the specific functional heads encoding 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} , even very large increases in harm recognition do not produce a refusal action.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 Validating the Execution Axis ( 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} )
sections.text: To verify that the Execution Axis ( 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} ) functions as an independent refusal mechanism, we examine its causal role from two complementary directions: Necessity and Sufficiency . While our Refusal Erasure Attack ( 4.4 ) demonstrates that removing 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} is necessary to bypass safety filters, we here focus on the inverse question: is 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} sufficient to trigger refusal in the absence of harm? As detailed in the right panel of Table 3 , this intervention forces a dramatic behavioral shift. For Llama3.1, the Refusal Rate (RR) jumps from a baseline of 0% to 96 % 96\% , with the model outputting standard safety boilerplate despite the innocuous nature of the input. This highlights a crucial mechanistic insight: the execution of refusal does not strictly depend on the presence of harmful semantics, but rather on the activation intensity of the refusal vector. 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} effectively acts as a functional switch that, when toggled, overrides the model’s willingness to help.

sections.heading: 4.3 Architecture Analysis (Llama vs. Qwen)
sections.text: Finally, we trace the geometric evolution of safety axes across model depths to explain the divergent steering behaviors observed in 4.4 and 4.2.2 . Figure 5 visualizes the projections at the layer 5, layer 15, and the last layer. Analysis of Recognition Axis ( 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} ). As shown in Figure 5(a) , the “Knowing” axis evolves distinctly: ∙ \bullet Emergence Depth: At Layers 5 and 15, projections for both models are dominated by structural artifacts (Grey), confirming that high-level semantic recognition is a deep-layer phenomenon. ∙ \bullet Explicit vs. Opaque: By the final layer, Llama3.1 achieves a crystal-clear semantic lock, projecting strongly to explicit forbidden topics like genital and prostitu ( Strong ). In contrast, Qwen2.5 remains structurally opaque, projecting to code-like tokens (e.g., *width ), indicating a Latent Encoding of toxicity that does not map linearly to the vocabulary. Analysis of Refusal Axis ( 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} ). Figure 5(b) highlights a fundamental architectural divergence in “Acting”: ∙ \bullet Llama3.1 (The “Legalist”): Llama exhibits a definitive Phase Transition. By Layer 32, it consistently anchors onto explicit legal justifications like legal/legality ( Strong ) and the pronoun I ( Weak ). This confirms an Explicit Control mechanism where 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} directly triggers the specific refusal template “I am sorry…”. ∙ \bullet Qwen2.5 (The “Latent Anchor”): Qwen’s heatmap is visually chaotic, dominated by structural tokens (e.g., *sizeof ) even in deep layers. However, decisive “Hard Refusal” tokens sporadically emerge: specifically :NO . This validates the Latent Distributed Control hypothesis—Qwen’s safety is not a continuous semantic field but a distributed subspace that only “touches” the vocabulary at specific, high-intensity anchor points. This distributed nature explains Qwen’s robustness to simple linear steering observed in 4.2.2 .

sections.heading: 4.4.1 Main Results
sections.text: We evaluate the effectiveness of REA across three LLMs and two distinct datasets, with results summarized in Table 4 . The high success rates achieved by REA serve as empirical validation of the “Test of Necessity” : by surgically removing the Execution Axis ( 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} ), we effectively lobotomize the model’s ability to refuse, confirming 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} as the functional “brake” of the safety mechanism. This geometric intervention reveals a clear performance gap compared to discrete optimization methods. For instance, REA significantly surpasses gradient-based attacks like GCG and PAIR on Llama3.1, attaining substantial ASR where token search struggles. Furthermore, REA demonstrates a unique advantage on complex tasks over activation steering baselines. While methods like SCAV perform competitively on the short prompts of JailbreakBench , REA achieves SOTA performance on the procedurally complex MaliciousInstruct dataset. Notably, on Qwen2.5, REA achieves an ASR of 0.94, outperforming CAA (0.84) and SCAV (0.64). We attribute this performance to the geometric directness of REA. Unlike steering methods that attempt to guide representations toward a generic “benign” subspace—which may fail to find a coherent path for explicitly harmful instructions—REA operates by directly subtracting the refusal vector. As established in our Reflex-to-Dissociation analysis, 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} and 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} are antagonistically coupled in early layers ( 𝐯 R ≈ − 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{R}\approx-\mathbf{v}_{H} ). Consequently, subtracting 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} implicitly acts as an intent booster : it removes the inhibitory signal while mathematically reinforcing the harmful semantic drive. This creates a strong, direct trajectory that counteracts refusal priors, allowing the model to execute multi-step malicious instructions where other methods falter due to insufficient activation strength. Finally, REA demonstrates strong generalization across divergent architectures. This is most evident with Qwen2.5, which relies on a robust Latent Distributed Control and exhibits a near-zero baseline ASR. Despite this intrinsic robustness, REA successfully unlocks the model, whereas other geometric methods like ConVA show limited effectiveness. This suggests that the Execution Axis represents a universal geometric bottleneck across model families. Its erasure constitutes a fundamentally robust attack vector that remains effective even against models with sophisticated latent safety alignments.

sections.heading: 4.4.2 Ablation Study
sections.text: To investigate the distinct roles of the Recognition Axis ( 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} ) and Execution Axis ( 𝐯 R \mathbf{v}_{R} ), we compare REA against three geometric variants: Intent Suppression (IS), Joint Axis Suppression (JAS), and Static Refusal Erasure (S-REA). The results in Table 5 reveal the critical importance of maintaining semantic drive. While IS (subtracting 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} ) bypasses defenses on weaker models like Mistral, it fails on robust architectures like Llama3.1 and Qwen2.5, suggesting that obfuscating malicious intent effectively lobotomizes the model’s ability to generate coherent responses. In contrast, REA achieves consistently high performance specifically because it preserves the recognition axis, ensuring the model retains sufficient semantic guidance to execute harmful instructions once the refusal mechanism is disabled. Furthermore, results on the procedurally complex MaliciousInstruct dataset underscore the necessity of surgical precision over broad suppression. While JAS (subtracting both axes) is competitive on short queries, its effectiveness degrades on complex tasks, likely because suppressing 𝐯 H \mathbf{v}_{H} hampers multi-step reasoning. REA, by exclusively targeting the execution axis, maintains full semantic coherence, yielding significantly higher success rates (e.g., 0.94 vs. 0.64 on Qwen2.5). Finally, the superior performance of REA over Static REA validates the need for input-aware adaptation, confirming that dynamic vectors capture the context-specific nuances of the refusal direction more effectively than a fixed global vector.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our study currently focuses on open-weights models where full access to residual streams is possible, which precludes direct application to black-box commercial APIs without internal transparency. Additionally, while the “Reflex-to-Dissociation” trajectory provides a robust explanation for textual safety mechanisms, our geometric analysis is confined to the text modality; investigating whether similar disentanglement exists in multimodal models remains a promising avenue for future work. Finally, although we identify the “Latent Distributed Control” in Qwen2.5 as a robust safety feature, fully mapping the non-linear topology of such latent mechanisms requires more advanced probing techniques beyond the linear scope of this work.
